sentences.text: Stegoceras was a small, bipedal dinosaur measuring 2 to 2.5 meters in length, a size comparable to that of a goat.
Its weight has been estimated to range between 10 and 40 kilograms.
Researchers suggest that the skull of this animal was flat in juveniles but developed a dome shape as the creature aged.
Like other pachycephalosaurs, Stegoceras would have possessed a small beak.
The first remains were collected by Lawrence Lambe from the Belly River Group in Alberta, Canada, and described in 1902.
Initial specimens included partial skull domes collected in 1898 and 1901, which Lambe used to name the genus Stegoceras and the species Stegoceras validum.
Stegoceras was likely herbivorous and probably possessed a good sense of smell.
The articulation between successive dorsal vertebrae prevented sideways movement, making the vertebral column very rigid and strengthened by ossified tendons.
The scapula was longer than the humerus, featuring a slender, narrow, and slightly twisted blade that followed the rib contour.
The type species of the genus Stegoceras is Stegoceras validum.
In 1978, Dong Zhiming classified Stegoceras within the family Pachycephalosauridae, which included dome-headed pachycephalosaurs.
In 1986, Paul Sereno grouped pachycephalosaurs like Stegoceras with ceratopsians into the suborder Marginocephalia based on cranial similarities.
A 2003 study by Sullivan suggested that Stegoceras was more primitive than fully-domed members of the subfamily Pachycephalosaurinae.
Stegoceras lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 77.5 to 74 million years ago.
Stegoceras validum is known from the Dinosaur Park and Oldman Formations, while S. novomexicanum is known from the Fruitland and Kirtland Formations.
Early researchers debated whether Stegoceras belonged to the ceratopsian or stegosaurian groups.
Franz Nopcsa doubted the association of the skull and skeleton, suggesting they belonged to different animals.
The species S. novomexicanum is debated and may not belong to the genus Stegoceras.
The function of the skull dome in Stegoceras is debated, with theories including combat, sexual display, or species recognition.
